title: The three-mile-an-hour God
hook: Kosuke Koyama: God walks at human pace, the speed of love

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Orthodox way, and a word for stillness: hesychia. Your line was the way of the heart. Did your attention drop from your head to your chest even once? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-three.

A rice field in the north of Thailand. A farmer is up to his shins in mud, behind a water buffalo that moves exactly as fast as a water buffalo wants to move. Standing at the edge of the field is a Japanese missionary and teacher named Kosuke Koyama. He has come to teach the Bible. He has books full of theology from Europe in his bag. And he starts to wonder whether he has been in too much of a hurry. What would the gospel sound like if it started here, in the mud, at the buffalo's pace? Out of those questions came a short book with an odd title, and that title is today's word.
screen: `A TEACHER WITH A BAG OF BOOKS.`

segments.voice: The book is called Three Mile an Hour God. Koyama's idea is simple enough to say in one breath: we walk at about three miles an hour, and so, he says, does God's love. It doesn't arrive by express train. It walks beside you. He starts in the wilderness. Moses tells the people of Israel, in the King James words: "thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart." Forty years, on foot. Koyama asks why God would take so long, and answers: because the lesson was trust, and trust can't be rushed. A people learning to depend on God one day of manna at a time. Second, Jesus. In the Gospels he goes from village to village, walking with his friends. And on the road to Emmaus, two grieving friends are trudging home when a stranger falls in beside them. Luke says: "Jesus himself drew near, and went with them." He doesn't fly in with the answer. He walks the long road at their pace, listening first. Third, the contrast. Koyama watched a world that prized speed: faster machines, faster results, faster everything. He didn't call speed evil. He said love has its own speed, and it's slow. You can't love someone at a hundred miles an hour. You have to stop, and look, and walk with them. Fourth, the buffalo again. The farmers he served weren't waiting for a theology flown in from somewhere else. Koyama tried to start from their life, their soil, their pace. That, he thought, is how God came to us: at walking speed, in the dust of one place.
screen: `WE WALK AT ABOUT THREE MILES AN HOUR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk slowly. If you can stand, stand up and take a few steps, much slower than usual, feeling each foot meet the floor. Heel, sole, toes. If you can't walk right now, just slow your breath to match an unhurried stride, in for one step, out for the next. Let your body find the speed of a person who isn't late for anything. If you pray, you can picture walking beside someone on a dusty road. If you don't, just notice what you see at this speed that you'd miss at a run. The bell holds the time.
The three-mile-an-hour God. Kosuke Koyama's picture of a love that walks at human pace, through the wilderness and down the Emmaus road.
Your line: the speed of love. Today, with one person, slow down on purpose: let them finish their sentence, walk at their pace, and don't check the time. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Some Christians practice slow walking prayer, on pilgrimage routes, in labyrinths or simply around a neighborhood, and some churches hold walks that retell the Emmaus road.

fork.reveal: Luke says "Jesus himself drew near, and went with them": he walks the road with them and listens first. that's Koyama's three-mile-an-hour God.

trapdoor: what you thought: God is fast, all-powerful, instant.
what it means: for Koyama, God's love moves at walking speed, the pace of trust and of being with someone.
what a scholar hears: Koyama taught in northern Thailand, and his title essay reads Deuteronomy 8's forty years in the wilderness as God teaching slowly, at walking pace.

notes: Koyama paraphrased throughout. Confirm: his missionary teaching in northern Thailand among rice farmers (Water Buffalo Theology); the 'three miles an hour' image (walking speed = the speed of love); his reading of the wilderness years as God teaching slowly.
The rice-field scene is a dramatized setting drawn from Water Buffalo Theology's opening, not a specific recorded moment; confirm acceptable.
'Forty years' is stated only as the quoted text says it (Deut 8:2). 'Three miles an hour' is from the book's title.
howItsDone mentions labyrinths and walking prayer generally; confirm acceptable.
